Joints
joynts
noun (plural)
From the Old French joint, past participle of joindre, to join, from the Latin jungere; rendering the Hebrew qatar (the knitting of the loins) and the Greek harmos and haphe, the fittings and the contact-points by which the body holds together.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The joints are where the frame holds together, and Scripture uses them for three things: terror, division, and union. In terror, Belshazzar’s joints are loosed. The hand writes upon the plaister of the wall and “the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another” (Dan 5:6) — a man who could hold a kingdom cannot hold his own body upright when God writes his sentence. In division, the joints mark the finest possible seam: the word of God is quick and powerful, “piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12). No blade reaches so far. Scripture separates what a man cannot separate in himself, cutting between motive and motive, and it does so as a discerner, not merely as a description. In union, the joints are the church’s. From Christ “the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth… maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love” (Eph 4:16), and the man who lets go the Head is severed from the body “which by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God” (Col 2:19). Every joint supplies; the body grows by contact, not by a member’s private vigour.

Webster 1828 Definition

The articulations at which bones and members are joined; in Scripture the seat of strength or of collapse, the finest seam the word of God divides, and the figure of the church’s knitting to its Head.

expand to see more

JOINT, n. The joining of two or more things; the place where two bodies or parts of a body are united.

Old French joint, from Latin jungere, to join.

In anatomy, an articulation; the seat of motion and of the body’s coherence.

Greek harmos, a fitting (Heb 4:12); haphe, a joint or point of contact by which supply passes (Eph 4:16; Col 2:19).

To be out of joint, or to have the joints loosed, is to lose all strength (Dan 5:6).

Key Scripture

Dan 5:6 — "Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another."

Heb 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

Eph 4:16 — "From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love."

Col 2:19 — "And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God."

Modern Corruption

The organic body of Eph 4:16 has been traded for a religion of spectators — Christianity without membership, without covenanted joints, without any obligation that a believer might actually be missed.

expand to see more

The corruption is a church without joints. It is now ordinary for people who profess Christ to hold no membership anywhere, to attend by preference and at a distance, and to describe this as faith unencumbered by institutions; the broadcast sermon replaces the assembly, the podcast replaces the elder, and no covenanted body knows whether the man is walking in the truth or has quietly stopped. Eph 4:16 does not permit the arrangement. The growth of the body comes by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part. A joint is a point of contact through which supply passes; a member joined to no one supplies nothing and receives nothing, whatever his opinions about the church universal. Col 2:19 states the danger at its worst: the one who does not hold the Head is cut off from the nourishment ministered by joints and bands. The New Testament knows no Christianity that is not embodied in a local congregation, under elders, at a table, with discipline — a joint fastened to other joints.

Recover the doctrine of union, in its two inseparable directions. First, union with Christ the Head: the body has no life, no supply, and no growth except from Him, and the increase it experiences is the increase of God, not the yield of programmes. Second, union with the members: joined together and compacted, which the Puritans understood as covenant membership with real obligations, real submission, and real love. Then let the other two uses of the joint do their work. Heb 4:12 keeps the assembly honest — the word divides the joints and marrow, and it discerns thoughts and intents, so no man sits under preaching merely as an observer; he is being opened. And Dan 5:6 keeps the confident sober. Belshazzar had a kingdom, a feast, and the vessels of the house of God on his table, and one line of divine handwriting loosed the joints of his loins. Strength held together by anything but Christ comes apart at the joints on the day it is tested.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The articulations that hold a frame together; in Scripture loosed in terror, divided by the word, and knit into one body under its Head.

expand to see more

Joints — Latin jungere, to join, through Old French joint.

Greek harmos, a fitting (Heb 4:12); haphe, a contact through which supply passes.

Dan 5:6 — the joints of the loins loosed: strength undone by a written sentence.

Heb 4:12 — the word divides joints and marrow, the finest seam in a man.

Eph 4:16 and Col 2:19 — the church grows by supply passing through every joint.

Usage

"Every joint supplieth: the body grows by contact, not by private vigour."

"Col 2:19 warns that not holding the Head cuts a man off from all nourishment."

"Belshazzar’s loosed joints show what a kingdom’s strength is worth under judgment."
